abstract: Oxytocin (OXT) is centrally involved in mammalian affiliation, but whether it modulates affiliative behavior toward artificial social agents, and how such an effect unfolds within a single interaction, is unclear. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo (PLA)-controlled study, 61 healthy adult males received 40 IU intranasal OXT or PLA before interacting with a Sony aibo robotic dog across an initial free interaction, a cooperative task-learning phase, and a final free interaction, with ten affiliative behaviors coded from video. OXT increased tactile engagement early: participants touched aibo longer during the initial free interaction, the only outcome of ten to survive family-wise correction. A weaker increase in smile frequency did not survive correction, and instrumental behavior was unaffected. Contrary to our second prediction, the advantage was not consolidated: it held through the initial interaction, closed across the intervening task, and was absent at the final one. An exploratory decomposition located the effect: participants under OXT did not initiate contact more often, and the difference was carried by how long each episode of contact was sustained. Urinary OXT confirmed group-level exposure. Because the design included no comparison condition and confounded interaction period with elapsed time and pharmacokinetics, it cannot establish bond formation, robot specificity, or consolidation as a psychological process. What it does bound is where and when OXT acted: on the maintenance of contact rather than its initiation, and only while the agent was novel, a pattern that fits salience- and novelty-based accounts better than bond formation.
